limitations: The construction is a reference prototype. The organiser requirement specifies primitives and goals, not a complete formal QDS protocol, and nothing here should be read as a specification of one.
Replay and identity checks are classical protocol controls. They are authorization bookkeeping, not quantum evidence, and they are reported separately for that reason.
Quantum measurement does not prove identity. A verified session is consistent with a calibrated honest model; it is not a proof of who sent it.

The simulator does not establish a new information-theoretic security proof, and no formal forgery bound is derived at this milestone. Deriving one is Milestone 6 work, and only if it is justified there.
Acceptance in the sampled measurement mode is a finite-shot outcome, not a deterministic property. The mode travels with every observation so the two are never conflated.
The statistical test is a consistency test against a calibrated honest model. A rejection is evidence of inconsistency with that model, not attribution of a cause.

FAR and FRR are empirical rates measured on the reported dataset. They depend on the modelled attacks, the modelled channel, the sample size and the error budget, and they do not transfer to other conditions.
The threshold is defined for one sample size. Applying it at another sample size is a category error, and the code raises rather than allowing it.
The multiple-comparison policy is one primary test with the remaining statistics reported as diagnostics. No joint acceptance region was derived, so no combined family-wise claim is made.
No machine learning is used anywhere. There is no learned threshold, no trained classifier and no anomaly model, so no result depends on a fitted model that could not be inspected.

measurement_configuration.why: the measurement mode decides whether the honest null is graded or degenerate, and the choice is therefore stated rather than left implicit. In 'projective-analytic' mode 'matched' means the received qubit is exactly the expected eigenstate, so any nonzero channel disturbance makes every state mismatch and the honest mismatch rate jumps from 0 to 1 with no interior for a finite-sample null. In 'sampled' mode with a large shot count the majority vote over many shots of a single qubit swamps small disturbance and the rate sits at 0 instead. 'sampled' mode with one shot per state is one measurement per qubit, which is what a verifier physically performs, and it gives a mismatch probability of 1 - p_match: a genuine interior null. This was established by measurement, not assumption; the three configurations were run over a noise sweep and their mismatch rates compared.

policy_notes: exactly one statistic is tested; its level is the operating point's alpha, with no family to correct for
every other Milestone 4 quantity is diagnostic evidence: reported, never adjudicated
a joint acceptance region over several statistics is not implemented, because no honest-model derivation of one has been done

provenance.profile_description: the recorded reference benchmark: one reference operating point, the eight reference curves, the attack evaluation, the noise grid and the discrimination experiment
profile_notes: trial counts are derived from a declared state budget rather than hand-picked; the quantity that costs time is trials x state_count, and holding it bounded keeps the study affordable while covering every simulatable design sample size
the reference channel is depolarizing at eta=0.02 with one measurement shot per state, which is the configuration in which the honest mismatch probability has a genuine interior value

the two largest design sample sizes (5000 and 10000) are above the reference protocol's maximum signature length of 4096 states, so they are declared as design values and have their thresholds derived exactly from the calibrated null, but they are not simulated: the protocol bound is not widened to make a benchmark reachable

transpile_cache.note: the cache stores compiled circuits keyed by a canonical circuit digest; it never stores outcomes. It is off by default and is proven result-preserving by tests/quantum/test_cache.py. The cache is disabled again once the run finishes, so enabled=False here would be wrong to read as 'the cache was not used'.

robustness.reading: honest_frr_by_noise is the honest false-rejection rate per noise level; detection_by_noise_and_attack is the share of malicious trials rejected at each noise level for each attack

sample_size.budget_note: trials and calibration sessions are derived from a declared state budget, so the trial count falls as the sample size rises; the simulated sample sizes are the simulatable subset of the declared design range
sample_size.exact_threshold_table_note: every row is derived exactly from the single reference calibration by the reference threshold method; 'simulated' says whether an evaluation was also run at that size. This is the answer to 'a threshold at N=100 is not valid at N=10,000': each row is that size's own threshold, and none of them is reused at another size
sample_size.note: each row's threshold is derived for that row's sample size only; the critical count is not comparable across rows as a rate without dividing by N
sample_size.unsimulated_reason: these design sizes exceed the reference protocol's maximum signature length of 4096 states, so an evaluation cannot be run at them. Their thresholds are derived exactly in 'exact_threshold_table' below, because a threshold is a binomial quantile of the calibrated null and needs no simulation; the protocol bound is deliberately not widened to make a run reachable
